hallmark: the dark fiddle across the pale wing cases, and the two yellow lines along the black pronotum

reference.title: Cetonia australasiae, from An epitome of the natural history of the insects of New Holland, plate 1

doc: *Eupoecila australasiae*, dorsal - the fiddler beetle.
Traced from plate 1 of Edward Donovan's *An epitome of the natural history
of the insects of New Holland* (1805), where it is figured and named
*Cetonia australasiae* - the description the species still carries, and the
reason this figure is its type. It is the same sheet the king Christmas
beetle came off, three figures away, so the two plates in this collection
that show Australian animals were drawn by one hand in one year.
`references/eupoecila-australasiae.jpg` is that figure, cut from the sheet
and turned upright.
## What identifies it
The **fiddle**: a dark field either side of the suture, broad at the
shoulder, waisted two thirds of the way down and closing at the apex, which
read across both wing cases at once is the outline of a violin. Then the
**two yellow lines** along the margins of an otherwise black pronotum -
which is the character Donovan's specific description opens with, before he
gets to the wing cases at all. Both are drawn.
## Which way round the animal is
The ground here is the *pale* colour and the pattern is dark on top of it,
which is the opposite of every other beetle in this collection. A fiddler
beetle is a yellow-green insect with a black figure on it, not a black
insect with yellow marks. Drawn the other way round it keys out on the same
six characters and looks like a different animal, so the fills are the
thing to check first if this plate is ever redrawn.
Donovan's hand-colouring makes the pale ground ferruginous - rust and ochre
- and his own Latin says *elytris ferrugineis*. The living animal is usually
lime-green to yellow. The plate is inked in one seasonal earth and takes no
position on which; `morphology.colourFamily` says `yellow`, which is what a
reader looking at the specimen would say, and the record's notes carry the
rest.
## Three colours, two pigments
The figure has a black field, a rust band and a pale margin. A plate has one
pigment at two strengths, so the rust band is drawn as a *boundary* rather
than as a fill - a structure-rank line along its outer edge. That is also
what carries the pattern at eighty pixels, where the detail rank has gone
and the fills have flattened.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front margin of the clypeus, y = 1000 at the apex of the wing
cases. There is no pygidium in this drawing: Donovan's figure rounds the
elytra off over it and shows none, and `REQUIRED_PARTS` does not ask a
beetle for an abdomen. The middle legs reach past x = 750.

note: Legs first, so they pass under the wing cases.
Slighter than the Christmas beetle's, and that is the point of drawing
the two together: both are scarabs, one digs and one visits flowers, and
the femora come out at about five and a half per cent of the width
across the wing cases against the other's eight. `eupoecila-australasiae
.plate.test.ts` measures both and asserts the difference, because a
proportion is only a fact when something else is beside it.
One wing case, pale. The ground colour is the light one here and the
pattern is drawn on top of it, which is the opposite of every other
beetle in the collection - see the fiddle below.
The fiddle. This is the identification and the reason the animal has the
name it has: a dark field either side of the suture, broad at the
shoulder, waisted at about two thirds of the way down and closing again
at the apex - the outline of a violin, laid across both wing cases at
once.
Drawn as ink on a pale ground rather than as a pale mark on a dark one,
because that is the way round the animal is built: a fiddler beetle is a
yellow-green beetle with a black pattern, not a black beetle with yellow
on it. Getting that backwards would have produced a plate that keys to
the same six characters and looks like a different insect.
The rust band that separates the black field from the pale margin.
A plate has two strengths of one pigment and this animal wants three
colours, so the third is drawn as a *boundary* rather than as a fill -
which is what an engraver working in one ink did with it too. The line
is what carries the fiddle's outer edge at small sizes; at eighty pixels
the fill has gone grey and this is all that is left of the pattern.
The reticulation. Donovan draws the pale part of each wing case as a
close net of engraved cells, several hundred of them; five strokes along
the margin is what survives of that at plate size.
The costae - the low longitudinal ribs a cetoniine's wing case carries,
running the length of the pale field outside the fiddle. Four, and only
on the pale side: on the dark field they would be invisible on the animal
and noise on the plate.
The dark field carried three of its own for one pass and lost the waist
under them. What identifies this animal is the *shape* of that field, so
it is left flat and every stroke on this wing case sits outside it.
The suture, drawn once on the axis. Reflecting it would lay a second copy
a hair off the first and show as a doubled line.
The pronotum, and the one part of this plate filled with the deep pigment
rather than the pale: it is black on the animal, and it is black in every
figure of it. The yellow margins are laid over it below.
The yellow along each side of the pronotum - two lines, in Donovan's own
words, and the character his specific description opens with, before he
gets to the wing cases at all.
Filled `pigment` and not `surface`, which is the more truthful of the two
and reads better as well. The yellow along this shield is the *same*
yellow as the wing cases, so it wants the same fill they have; bare paper
made two hard white patches on a black ground that read as a second pair
of eyes.
A `strip` rather than a closed curve. Drawn as an outer chain of points
and an inner one, the smoothing bows each corner outward and the band
came out half the width of the shield - two white eyes rather than two
margins. A strip offsets along the measured edge's own normal, which is
what a band following a margin actually is.
The head. Narrow and squared off in front, where the Christmas beetle's
is a broad shovel - the difference between a scarab that digs and one
that feeds at flowers, and visible in dorsal view without a lens.
Donovan draws it cocked about ten pixels to the animal's right, as he
does the Christmas beetle's. Drawn square here for the same reason.
A lamellate club, as on every scarab. Drawn as one filled club with two
lines across it rather than as three separate plates, which at plate size
would be three smudges.
